title: Fractional & Small Interests
metaTitle: Selling Small Fractional Mineral Interests in Colorado
metaDescription: Own a tiny fractional Colorado mineral interest split among many heirs? We buy small undivided shares that are too small for most buyers to bother with.
heroLead: A 1/64th undivided interest split three generations deep isn't worth much to hold and manage, and it's usually the exact kind of tract most buyers skip past.
intro: Colorado's oldest producing areas, particularly parts of Weld County and the DJ Basin, have been through enough decades of inheritance, subdivision, and re-division that many mineral interests are now held in fractions like 1/32nd or 1/128th of the original tract, split across cousins, aunts, and heirs who may not even know each other. These fractional interests generate royalty checks small enough that some owners describe them as more of a nuisance than an asset.

We buy fractional and small undivided interests specifically because most institutional buyers set a minimum size and won't bother underwriting anything below it. A tiny check every month or quarter still represents a real, sellable ownership stake, and we quote it the same way we'd quote a larger interest: against actual production history and offset activity, scaled to your fraction.

sections.heading: Why fractional interests get overlooked
paragraphs: Most buyers in the mineral acquisition space set a floor on deal size because the title work, division order confirmation, and closing costs are roughly the same whether the interest is 1/4 or 1/256. That fixed cost makes very small interests unattractive to buyers focused on larger deals, which leaves fractional owners with few options beyond holding an interest that generates a small check and periodic paperwork.
We work these deals in volume, often alongside other family members' fractions from the same original tract, which makes small individual interests worth underwriting properly rather than passing on.

sections.heading: Confirming your exact fraction
paragraphs: The fraction on your division order statement reflects your net revenue interest after generations of division, and it isn't always intuitive from the original deed language. We pull the chain of title at the county clerk's office to confirm your fraction independently, which matters because inherited fractional interests sometimes carry small discrepancies between what heirs believe they own and what the recorded instruments actually show.

If your interest has never been formally probated or transferred into your name after an inheritance, that gap needs to be resolved before a sale can close cleanly, and we can walk you through what's needed rather than leaving you to figure out probate requirements alone.

sections.heading: Selling alongside other heirs, or on your own
paragraphs: You don't need every co-owner of the original tract to agree before selling your own fractional share; a Colorado mineral interest can be sold by one heir independently of the others. That said, we're happy to coordinate a single closing if multiple family members with fractions from the same tract want to sell together, which can simplify title work for everyone and is often more efficient than separate transactions.

sections.heading: Why small checks still deserve a real valuation
paragraphs: A fractional interest paying a modest amount each quarter is easy to dismiss as too small to bother pricing carefully, but the underlying math is identical to a larger interest: decline curve, offset activity, and remaining well life scaled down to your fraction. We build that same analysis for a 1/128th interest as we would for a full undivided tract, because skipping the work just because the check is small tends to produce an unfair lowball number for the owner.

If your fraction traces to a tract with active current drilling, even a small interest can be worth pursuing a sale on now rather than continuing to collect scattered, hard-to-track quarterly payments for years to come.

sections.heading: When fractions come from multiple original tracts
paragraphs: Some heirs end up holding several unrelated fractional interests, small pieces of different family tracts acquired or inherited at different points, sometimes in different counties entirely. Managing several small royalty streams from different operators, each with its own division order quirks and reporting schedule, is often more administrative burden than the combined income justifies.
We're glad to review a full list of scattered fractional holdings together and quote them as a package where that makes sense, rather than requiring a separate conversation for each individual tract.

faqs.question: Is my interest too small to sell?
faqs.answer: Probably not to us. We regularly buy interests as small as a fraction of a percent, which most larger buyers won't underwrite because the fixed costs of title work don't scale down with deal size.

faqs.question: How do I find out my exact fraction?
faqs.answer: Your division order check stub usually shows a decimal interest. We independently confirm that fraction against the recorded chain of title before closing, since inherited fractions occasionally carry discrepancies.

faqs.question: Do all the heirs who share the original tract need to sell together?
faqs.answer: No. Each heir's fractional interest can be sold independently. We can also coordinate a single closing for multiple family members if that's easier for everyone.

faqs.question: My inherited interest was never formally transferred into my name. Can I still sell?
faqs.answer: That needs to be resolved first, typically through probate or an affidavit of heirship depending on your situation. We can explain what's needed for your specific case before we proceed to closing.
